Many censored subjects

Source: vignettes/articles/censored-subjects.Rmd
censored-subjects.Rmd

The backward joint model factorizes the joint distribution as f(T)f(Y∣T)f(T)\,f(Y \mid T). The usual fit estimates the longitudinal sub-model f(Y∣T)f(Y \mid T) on the subjects with an observed event, since only they have a known TT. Prediction, however, needs f(Y∣T)f(Y \mid T) for every TT after the prediction time. When many subjects are censored, the events are mostly early ones, so for a patient who is doing well the event-time effect is extrapolated well beyond the event times it was estimated from. With a term linear in TT, this pulls the predictive distribution of TT towards early events: predicted risks are too high, and more so at later landmarks, where the patients still at risk are the long survivors.

predictRisk() warns (once per session) when the longitudinal fit has no more subjects than the survival fit has events while at least 30% of the subjects are censored.

Using the censored subjects

A censored subject’s history says that T>CT > C and how the biomarkers behaved until CC, which is exactly the information about long event times that the events-only fit leaves out. fitImputedBJM() uses it: it draws each censored subject’s TT from f(T∣T>C,Y,X)∝f(Y∣T,X)f(T∣X)f(T \mid T > C, Y, X) \propto f(Y \mid T, X) f(T \mid X) (with competing risks, TT and the event type jointly), refits longitudinalSub() on everyone, iterates, and pools several imputations, as fitIntervalBJM() does for interval censoring.

Once the censored subjects are in the fit, the event-time effect is estimated over long event times too, and a term linear in TT can drift over them. A bounded effect such as exp⁡(−T/κ)\exp(-T/\kappa) levels off instead. Write it in place of years in every term:

library(BJM)
data(pbc3)
pbc3_surv <- pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ]
fixed <- function(b, kappa) {
  G <- sprintf("I(exp(-years/%g))", kappa)
  as.formula(sprintf(paste0("%s ~ year + age + sex + %2$s + year:%2$s + status4 + status4:year + ",
                            "status4:%2$s + status4:year:%2$s"), b, G))
}
biomarkers <- c("serBilir", "albumin", "prothrombin")
fit_kappa <- function(kappa) {
  fx <- lapply(biomarkers, fixed, kappa = kappa)
  rd <- rep(list(~ year | id), 3)
  names(fx) <- names(rd) <- biomarkers
  fitImputedBJM(pbc3_surv, pbc3, Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, fx, rd, "year",
                form_conditional_cr = status4 ~ years + age + sex, seed = 1)
}
fits <- lapply(c(2, 5, 10), fit_kappa)

Choosing the form of the event-time effect

observedLongLogLik() gives the observed-data log-likelihood of the longitudinal sub-model: log⁡f(Y∣T,D)\log f(Y \mid T, D) for a subject with an event, log⁡∫C∞∑df(Y∣t,d)P(d∣t)dF(t)−log⁡S(C)\log \int_C^\infty \sum_d f(Y \mid t, d) P(d \mid t)\,dF(t) - \log S(C) for a censored one. Fits sharing the survival sub-model can be compared on it; higher is better.

sapply(fits, observedLongLogLik, data_survival = pbc3_surv, data_fit_all = pbc3,
       time_variable = "year")

On pbc3, κ=5\kappa = 5 has the highest log-likelihood (about −1670-1670, against −1690-1690 to −1720-1720 for 2 and 10, and −2010-2010 for the usual linear fit on the events).

What it changes on pbc3

Predicted over observed 3-year cumulative incidence of death (transplant competing; Aalen-Johansen), 5-fold cross-validation, 3 biomarkers:

Landmark (years) 1 2 3
Usual fit (events only, linear in years) 1.08 1.14 1.32
fitImputedBJM(), exp⁡(−T/5)\exp(-T/5) 0.99 1.02 1.07

The AUC is unchanged (within 0.01). Most of the correction comes from using the censored subjects; the bounded form keeps it from depending on how far a linear term is extrapolated.

Beyond the last follow-up

The draws of TT beyond the last follow-up, and any prediction reaching there, rest on the survival sub-model’s baseline hazard, which survivalSub() can only extrapolate. When an external cohort with longer follow-up is available (an earlier generation of a device, a registry), survivalSubExternal() fits one Cox model to both with a generation indicator, so the study’s hazard there is the external one scaled by a hazard ratio. It needs proportional hazards between the cohorts, also where only the external cohort is observed; the cox.zph test it runs on the overlap has little power with short follow-up, so treat the borrowed tail as an assumption to vary in a sensitivity analysis.

# sketch: study_surv / study_long are the study (one row per subject / long format),
# external_surv the external cohort (one row per subject, no biomarkers needed);
# fx, rd as above
surv_ext <- survivalSubExternal(study_surv, external_surv, Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex)
surv_ext$external$ph_test
fit <- fitImputedBJM(study_surv, study_long, Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, fx, rd, "year",
                     survival_fit_all = surv_ext)

The whole predictive distribution of TT

predictEventTime() returns, for each patient, the CDF of TT at several horizons and its quantiles in one pass. The 10% quantile, for example, is a time the patient outlives with probability 0.9 – a lower prediction bound for durability.

history <- pbc3[pbc3$id %in% c(2, 7) & pbc3$year <= 3, ]
history$years <- NA
history$status4 <- NA
predictEventTime(history, fits[[2]]$long_fit_all, fits[[2]]$survival_fit_all,
                 prediction_time = 3, horizons = c(1, 3, 5), time_variable = "year",
                 probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
